lead: Quality is built in while work is done, not inspected in at the end. Software quality assurance (SQA) is the planned set of activities — standards, reviews, audits and measurements — that checks the process, not just final code. Technical reviews are the cheapest: a small group reads a design or module and logs defects before any test case is written. Below: the SQA process, three review types and their roles, and the numbers that show whether a review paid off.
prereq: You need verification and validation, QA versus QC (Unit 4, Software Testing Strategies and Techniques), and measurement ideas in 6.2.

sections.h3: The SQA process, and QA versus QC

blocks.text: SQA looks at how software is built; quality control (QC) looks at the product: testing a build, timing a response, running a static analyser. Both are needed. QC asks "does this product meet its specification?" SQA asks "is our process capable of producing such a product?"
The SQA group does five kinds of work.

items: Plan. Write the SQA plan: which work products are reviewed, by whom, against which standard, and when; it sits inside the project plan of 6.1.
Standards. Keep a short list the team follows — naming rules, coding style, document templates, review checklists.
Reviews and audits. Chair technical reviews; audit whether the documented process was followed on a real project.
Records. Log defects, review hours and test results so trends are visible, not just single numbers.
Configuration. Ensure every reviewed product is baselined and change-controlled, as in 6.6.

blocks.text: Process standards say how work must be done; ISO 9001 and CMMI maturity levels (1 to 5) are examples, and suppliers claim conformance to win contracts. Product standards say what a deliverable looks like, such as an SRS template or Java style guide.

An SQA group that only writes documents and never reads a real design is decoration. Its authority comes from one power: it can stop a work product moving to the next phase until the review record is closed.

sections.h3: Technical reviews: informal review, walkthrough and inspection

blocks.text: A technical review is a structured reading of a work product by people other than the author — requirements, design, code, test plans or user documents — before testing. Three forms are common.
Informal review. A colleague reads your code or design at the desk. No agenda, no record. Cheap and useful for a 50-line function; useless as evidence.

Walkthrough. The author leads the group through the document step by step; the group asks questions and notes problems. Its purpose is education as much as detection: new members learn the design, and the author often spots errors while explaining. A formal defect list is not mandatory.

Inspection. The most formal form, with defined roles. A moderator schedules and runs it; the product is walked through by the moderator or a nominated reader, not the author, who stays silent except to answer questions of intent. Three to six reviewers prepare alone with a checklist; a recorder writes down every defect. The flow is planning, overview, preparation, inspection meeting, rework, follow-up.

items: Moderator plans the meeting, keeps time, decides pass or rework.
Author supplies material, answers intent questions, fixes defects.
Reviewer prepares in advance and hunts defects against the checklist, not style preferences.
Recorder logs each defect with location, type and severity.

blocks.text: A checklist stops reviewers drifting. Typical lines: is every requirement traceable to a design element? are all inputs validated? are error paths handled? are units named consistently? Ten to twenty items grown from past defects beat a hundred-line list nobody reads.
Each defect goes into a log with id, location (page, section, line), description, type (missing, wrong, extra), severity and status. The log is the review's output and proof.
Reviews produce numbers that say whether to keep reviewing this way.

blocks.where: R is review rate in lines per hour; L is product size in lines; H is total reviewer-hours = number of reviewers × hours each spent. Typical inspection rates are 100–200 lines of code per hour, slower for design. Above that, detection falls sharply.

D is defect density in defects per KLOC; D<sub>r</sub> is defects found in review; D<sub>t</sub> is defects found later in testing; K is size in KLOC. Counting only review defects flatters the process.

E is review effectiveness, the share of all defects the review caught. If a review finds 20 and testing later finds 4, E = 20 ÷ 24 × 100% = 83.33%. High E means reviews do work testing would otherwise do, and a review defect costs a fraction of one caught in system test.

figure.caption: A formal inspection moves from planning and overview to preparation, the meeting where defects are logged, rework by the author, and follow-up to confirm every defect is closed. The author does rework; the moderator owns follow-up.

spec.aria: A formal review moves from planning and overview to preparation, inspection, rework and follow-up.

examples.question: A 4,000-line module is inspected over 20 reviewer-hours. The inspection finds 20 defects; testing later finds 4 more in the same module. Compute review rate, defect density after all defects, and review effectiveness.
steps: Rate: R = L ÷ H = 4,000 ÷ 20 = 200 lines per hour, at the top of the normal 100–200 band.
examples.answer: Review rate = 200 lines per hour, defect density = 6 defects per KLOC, and review effectiveness = 83.33%.
examples.check:
lines = 4000
hours = 20
review_defects = 20
test_defects = 4
review_rate = lines / hours
kloc = lines / 1000
density = (review_defects + test_defects) / kloc
effectiveness = round(review_defects / (review_defects + test_defects) * 100, 2)
print(review_rate)
print(density)
print(effectiveness)

traps: SQA is not testing. Testing is QC on the product; SQA checks process and work products and runs alongside testing.
Walkthrough and inspection differ: inspection is formal with roles, preparation and a defect log.
Review rate divides lines by reviewer-hours, not calendar hours. Five reviewers for 4 hours is 20 reviewer-hours, so 4,000 lines gives 200 lines per hour, not 1,000.
Review effectiveness uses review plus later testing defects. Dividing by review defects alone always gives 100%.
Defect density is per KLOC. Reporting 0.006 per line when 6 per KLOC is expected loses marks even with right arithmetic.

quiz.q: Define SQA and state one way it differs from quality control.
quiz.a: SQA is the planned set of activities that assure the process will produce quality software: standards, reviews, audits, records. QC works on the product itself, e.g. testing a build. SQA is process-oriented; QC is product-oriented.

quiz.q: Why does an inspection team use a checklist instead of reading the document freely?
quiz.a: A checklist focuses every reviewer on defect types that have hurt before — missing requirements, unvalidated inputs, unhandled error paths. It makes coverage repeatable across reviewers and sessions and can be updated from past defect data. A 10–20 item list is used; a long one is skipped.

quiz.q: A 3,000-line module is inspected by 5 reviewers, each spending 2 hours. Find the review rate and say what it implies.
quiz.a: H = 5 × 2 = 10 reviewer-hours. R = 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300 lines per hour. That is above the normal 100–200 band, so detection is likely poor; add reviewer-hours or split the module.

quiz.q: Team A has review effectiveness 60% and Team B has 85%, with the same number of defects injected per KLOC. Which team ships more escaped defects, and why?
quiz.a: Team A. Escaped defects are the share not caught in review: 40% for A against 15% for B. With identical injection rates, A carries about 2.7 times as many defects into testing and release, shifting cost into system test and field support.

quiz.q: Name the four roles in a formal inspection and give one duty of each.
quiz.a: Moderator: plans and runs the meeting, decides pass or rework. Author: supplies the product, answers intent questions, does rework. Reviewer: prepares in advance and finds defects with the checklist. Recorder: writes each defect with location, type and severity into the log.

quiz.q: Why is a defect found in a technical review cheaper than the same defect found in system testing?
quiz.a: In a review the defect is a log line and a small edit before the code enters a testable release. In system testing it has propagated into other modules; testers must reproduce it, a build must be reissued and tests rerun, so rework and re-verification multiply the cost.

quiz.q: A 2,500-line module shows 15 defects in inspection and 5 more in testing. Compute the defect density and the review effectiveness.
quiz.a: K = 2,500 ÷ 1,000 = 2.5 KLOC. Total defects = 15 + 5 = 20, so D = 20 ÷ 2.5 = 8 defects per KLOC. E = 15 ÷ 20 × 100% = 75%.

quiz.q: Why does a defect log record location, type and severity rather than just a count?
quiz.a: Location lets the author fix it fast and shows weak sections or modules. Type (missing, wrong, extra) reveals mistake patterns, suggesting checklist items and process fixes. Severity decides what must be fixed before the product moves on and what can wait, so the moderator can judge pass or rework.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most teams now use pull requests: a reviewer reads a diff and blocks the change until comments are resolved. Static analysers and linters catch mechanical defects, freeing humans for logic and design. Research tracks how coverage, reviewer load and speed predict escaped defects; defect prediction ranks files by risk so review time pays. Search for "modern code review", "defect prediction", "static analysis in CI" and "software quality metrics defect density".
